lessons.title: The Administrative State and the APA
body: Administrative law is the body of law that governs the agencies of government: how they are created, what powers they hold, what procedures they must follow, and how courts and other branches check them. Most of the law that touches daily life, from food safety to workplace rules to benefits, is made and applied by agencies rather than by Congress or courts directly. Lawyers call this the administrative state.

An agency is a governmental body that exercises authority delegated by statute. Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) of 1946, an agency is broadly any authority of the federal government other than Congress, the federal courts, and a few listed bodies. The Supreme Court held in Franklin v. Massachusetts (1992) that the President is not an agency for APA purposes, so presidential action is not reviewable under the APA even though the actions of the agencies he directs are.

The key principle is that an agency has only the power Congress gives it. Agencies are created by an organic or enabling statute that states their mission and authority. An agency action that goes beyond that grant is ultra vires, meaning beyond its powers, and a court will set it aside. Agencies have no inherent authority the way a legislature or a court does.

The federal system grew in waves. The Interstate Commerce Commission (1887) and the Federal Trade Commission (1914) were early regulators of industry. The New Deal added the Securities and Exchange Commission, the National Labor Relations Board and many others. A later wave in the 1960s and 1970s produced the Environmental Protection Agency, OSHA and similar health, safety and environmental bodies. The APA was Congress's attempt, after the New Deal, to give all of these agencies a common procedural code.

Agencies come in two structural families. Executive departments, such as Justice or Treasury, are headed by officials whom the President may remove at will. Independent agencies, such as the Federal Trade Commission, are typically led by a multimember board, with statutory limits on the President's power to remove its members, often for cause only. Later lessons show that this difference has been reshaped by the Supreme Court's recent removal decisions, which now let the President remove the heads of agencies that wield executive power, such as the FTC, at will.

Agencies combine functions that the Constitution separates among branches. They make rules that bind like statutes (legislative function), decide individual cases (judicial function), and investigate and prosecute (executive function). The APA's central distinction follows the first two: a rule is an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect, and an order is the final disposition of a matter other than rulemaking, which usually comes from adjudication. Much of the course turns on whether an agency used the right procedure for the kind of action it took.

Worked example: Congress passes a statute telling an agency to set safe levels of a workplace chemical. The agency drafts a standard, takes public comment and issues it as a rule. Later it fines a particular employer for violating the standard, which is adjudication. A court asked to review either action first asks whether the agency stayed within the statute, then whether it followed the proper procedure, and then whether its reasoning was lawful.

lessons.title: Delegation and the Nondelegation Doctrine
body: Article I, Section 1 of the Constitution vests all legislative powers in Congress. Agencies make rules that function like laws, so the nondelegation doctrine asks whether Congress may transfer that rule-making power to someone else. If Congress could pass a statute that simply says make whatever rules are good for the country, the separation of powers would mean little.

The Court has never said Congress cannot delegate. Chief Justice Taft stated the modern test in J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States (1928): Congress may confer discretion if it lays down an intelligible principle to which the delegate must conform. The statute must tell the agency what the policy goal is and set boundaries, so a court can check whether the agency stayed inside them. The idea is that filling in details is permissible, whereas making the basic policy choices is for Congress.

The doctrine has been enforced in only two cases, both in 1935. In Panama Refining Co. v. Ryan the Court struck down a provision that let the President ban certain oil shipments without any standard to guide him. In A.L.A. Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States it struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act's authority to approve codes of fair competition, which had almost no limiting standard. Since then the Court has upheld standards as broad as a rule that agencies act in the public interest, convenience or necessity, and the standard that an air quality standard be requisite to protect the public health with an adequate margin of safety (Whitman v. American Trucking Associations, 2001). Mistretta v. United States (1989) upheld the delegation to the Sentencing Commission, noting that in our complex society Congress must be able to delegate.

The doctrine seemed settled until Gundy v. United States (2019). Congress had authorized the Attorney General to specify how the sex offender registry law applied to people convicted before the law passed. A four-Justice plurality, with Justice Kagan writing, applied the intelligible principle test and upheld it. Justice Alito concurred in the judgment, but said he would be willing to reconsider the doctrine in a future case. Justice Gorsuch, in dissent for three, proposed a stricter test. Justice Kavanaugh later wrote that Gorsuch's approach deserved further consideration, which signalled interest among several Justices.

In FCC v. Consumers' Research (2025) the Court upheld the Universal Service Fund's funding scheme against a nondelegation challenge, applying the intelligible principle framework and rejecting the argument that the statute left the agency unconstrained. The majority did not abandon the test. The opinion also rejected a separate challenge based on the idea that a private entity assisted the agency, because the agency remained in control. As of this writing the intelligible principle test remains the law, with several Justices open to revisiting it.

Courts have worked around the issue through two tools. The canon of constitutional avoidance leads courts to read broad grants narrowly so that the statute does not violate nondelegation. Related to this is the major questions doctrine, covered in a later lesson. Private delegations are a different problem: Carter v. Carter Coal Co. (1936) invalidated giving private parties power to set wages and hours for competitors, and the Court has said that private bodies may not wield government power with no governmental control.

Worked example: A statute says the Secretary shall issue such regulations as the Secretary finds necessary and in the public interest, with no other direction. Under the Hampton test a challenger would argue there is no intelligible principle, but courts have upheld equally open-ended phrases, so the challenge would likely fail under current doctrine, though it would draw interest.

lessons.title: Appointment and Removal: Presidential Control of Personnel
body: Article II vests the executive power in the President and tells him to take care that the laws be faithfully executed. Two constitutional provisions shape the personnel question. The Appointments Clause says principal officers are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate, while Congress may by law vest the appointment of inferior officers in the President alone, the courts of law, or heads of departments. The Constitution is silent on removal, so the rules come from case law.

Who is an officer? A person who exercises significant authority under federal law in a continuing position is an officer (Buckley v. Valeo, 1976). Lucia v. SEC (2018) applied that to administrative law judges in the SEC, holding that they are officers whose appointment by agency staff rather than by the Commission violated the clause. Inferior officers are those whose work is directed and supervised by a principal officer (Edmond v. United States, 1997).

Removal is the harder subject. In Myers v. United States (1926) the Court held that the President could remove a postmaster without Senate consent, endorsing a broad executive removal power. Nine years later Humphrey's Executor v. United States (1935) upheld a statute that protected FTC commissioners from removal except for inefficiency, neglect of duty or malfeasance. The Court reasoned that the FTC exercised quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial powers and so could be insulated from the President. Morrison v. Olson (1988) upheld for-cause protection for an independent counsel, replacing the quasi test with a question of whether the removal limit impedes the President's ability to perform his constitutional duties.

The modern Court narrowed Humphrey's and then overruled it. Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB (2010) struck down two layers of for-cause protection between the President and board members. Seila Law LLC v. CFPB (2020) held that Congress may not give a single director who wields significant executive power protection from at-will removal, and described Humphrey's as limited to multimember expert bodies that do not wield substantial executive power. Collins v. Yellen (2021) applied the same reasoning to the Federal Housing Finance Agency's director. Before 2026 these cases described two exceptions: multimember expert bodies, and inferior officers with limited duties.

The newest chapter is the most important. In 2025 the President removed members of the National Labor Relations Board and the Merit Systems Protection Board, and the Supreme Court granted interim stays allowing the removals (Trump v. Wilcox, 2025), while noting that the Federal Reserve is a uniquely structured quasi-private entity. The Court then took up the removal of an FTC commissioner. On June 29, 2026, in Trump v. Slaughter, it ruled six to three, in an opinion by Chief Justice Roberts, that Humphrey's Executor is overruled. The FTC exercises executive power through rulemaking, enforcement and litigation, so the President may remove its commissioners at will. The opinion also left open that the Federal Reserve, with its distinct historical tradition, may be treated differently.
Remedy matters too. Even when a removal restriction is unconstitutional, the Court has treated it as severable, so the agency continues to exist and its past actions are not automatically void. Collins held that a challenger must show the restriction actually harmed them.

Worked example: A statute creates a five-member commission and says commissioners may be removed only for good cause. Under Trump v. Slaughter, a court would ask whether the body exercises executive power, such as rulemaking and enforcement. If it does, the for-cause limit cannot bind the President and he may remove a commissioner at will. Only a body exercising no part of the executive power, or the Federal Reserve with its distinct history, might still be protected, a question the Court left open.

lessons.title: Presidential and Congressional Oversight Tools
body: Control of agencies runs through two political branches, each with tools that the courts have shaped.

For the President, the central tool is centralized regulatory review. Since Executive Order 12291 (1981) and its successor, Executive Order 12866 (1993), significant rules from executive agencies are reviewed by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), part of the Office of Management and Budget, before they issue. The order requires a cost-benefit analysis for significant rules and asks agencies to select approaches that maximize net benefits to the extent permitted by law. Independent agencies were historically outside this requirement, though recent administrations have sought to extend review to them. Executive Order 14215, Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies (February 18, 2025), directed independent regulatory agencies to submit proposed and final significant regulatory actions to OIRA before publication, with the Federal Reserve's monetary policy functions exempted. Trump v. Slaughter (2026), which confirmed the President's power to remove the heads of agencies that exercise executive power at will, supports that kind of presidential supervision.

Executive orders and memoranda direct how the executive branch carries out statutes. They are law-like only within the executive branch and only if they rest on constitutional or statutory authority. Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952) is the foundational limit: the Court held that President Truman could not seize steel mills during the Korean War without statutory authority. Justice Jackson's concurrence set out three categories: presidential power is at its peak when Congress has authorized the action, in a zone of twilight when Congress is silent, and at its lowest ebb when the President acts against the will of Congress.

Congress has several tools. It controls the agency's budget and mission through appropriations, holds oversight hearings, confirms principal officers, and can amend the organic statute. It may also require reports.

The legislative veto was an attempt to let Congress undo agency action without passing a new statute. INS v. Chadha (1983) held that a one-house veto of an immigration decision was unconstitutional because it was legislative in effect and so had to comply with bicameralism and presentment, meaning passage by both houses and presentation to the President. Bowsher v. Synar (1986) added that Congress may not keep removal power over an executive officer, and so the Comptroller General could not execute the deficit control law.

The Congressional Review Act (CRA) of 1996 works within Chadha. Agencies must submit major rules to Congress, and Congress can pass a joint resolution of disapproval, which the President can veto. A resolution that becomes law invalidates the rule and bars the agency from issuing a substantially the same rule without new congressional authority. It was used only once before 2017, but it has been used much more since, mostly when party control of the White House changes. Courts generally do not review whether Congress properly used the CRA, since the statute bars judicial review of congressional determinations.

Worked example: An agency issues a significant rule shortly before a new administration takes office. The new Congress passes a CRA resolution and the new President signs it. The rule is void, and the agency cannot reissue a substantially similar rule unless a later statute authorizes it. The same result could not be reached by a one-house vote, because Chadha requires presentment.

lessons.title: Informal (Notice-and-Comment) Rulemaking
body: Most federal rules are made through informal rulemaking, also called notice-and-comment rulemaking, governed by section 553 of the APA. The sequence has three core steps. First, the agency publishes a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register stating the time, place and nature of the proceeding, the legal authority for the rule, and either the terms of the proposed rule or a description of the subjects and issues involved. Second, the agency gives interested persons an opportunity to participate by submitting written comments, with or without oral presentation. Third, after considering the relevant matter presented, the agency adopts the rule with a concise general statement of its basis and purpose.

The concise statement is, in practice, long. Courts have read the APA together with the arbitrary and capricious standard to require that the agency respond to significant comments and explain its reasoning, so that a reviewing court can see why the agency chose as it did. A final rule is published in the Federal Register and ordinarily takes effect no sooner than thirty days after publication (section 553(d)), with exceptions such as a rule that grants an exemption or relieves a restriction.

The final rule must be a logical outgrowth of the proposal. Notice must be fair, so that interested people could anticipate the change that the agency finally makes. An agency may change a rule between proposal and adoption in response to comments, but if the final rule is so different that a reasonable commenter would not have realized it was on the table, the notice was inadequate. Long Island Care at Home, Ltd. v. Coke (2007) states the logical outgrowth idea in the course of upholding a rule.

Several supplements exist outside the APA. Executive Order 12866 requires OIRA review of significant rules and a cost-benefit analysis. The Regulatory Flexibility Act requires the agency to assess the effect of rules on small entities. The Paperwork Reduction Act controls information collection. Statutes like the National Environmental Policy Act can require a separate environmental review. The Federal Advisory Committee Act controls advice groups.

An important limit on courts is Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. NRDC (1978). The D.C. Circuit had required procedures beyond the APA's minimum, including extra hearing rights, as a condition of valid rulemaking. The Supreme Court reversed and held that courts may not impose procedural requirements that go beyond those the APA, the Constitution, or another statute require. Agencies are free to use more procedure, but courts may not demand it. After Vermont Yankee, courts police the quality of reasoning through arbitrary and capricious review rather than inventing new procedures.

Further, rulemaking may be initiated by a petition, since section 553(e) lets any interested person petition for the issuance, amendment or repeal of a rule. A denial of a petition is reviewable, though deferentially.

Agencies also may amend or repeal rules, and the APA treats that as rulemaking: the same procedures apply to repeal as to issuance. An agency that skips notice and comment to rescind a rule violates the APA.

Worked example: An agency proposes to limit emissions of a pollutant from coal plants at a level of 10 units. Comments from industry and public groups raise the cost of control and the health benefit. The final rule sets the limit at 8 units and adds a monitoring requirement not mentioned in the proposal. A challenger would say the monitoring requirement was not a logical outgrowth and the agency did not respond to the cost comments. The first argument could succeed if no reader of the proposal could have anticipated monitoring, and the second turns on whether the cost comment was significant.

lessons.title: Exemptions, Guidance and Legislative Rules
body: Section 553 does not apply to every agency action, and the exemptions are among the most tested topics in administrative law. The APA exempts rulemaking from the whole of section 553 for matters involving a military or foreign affairs function of the United States. Section 553(a)(2) also exempts matters relating to agency management or personnel or to public property, loans, grants, benefits or contracts, though many agencies have waived that exemption by their own rules.

Within section 553(b), notice and comment is not required for interpretive rules, general statements of policy, and rules of agency organization, procedure or practice. It is also excused for good cause, when the agency finds for good cause, and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of the reasons into the rule, that notice and public procedure are impracticable, unnecessary or contrary to the public interest. Courts read good cause narrowly. An emergency, a statutory deadline that leaves no time, or a purely technical change that no one could object to may qualify.

The central distinction is between legislative rules and the rest. A legislative rule, also called a substantive rule, is issued under delegated authority and has the force and effect of law. Chrysler Corp. v. Brown (1979) states that a properly promulgated legislative rule can bind like a statute. It must come out of notice and comment unless an exemption applies. An interpretive rule instead advises the public of the agency's construction of statutes and rules it administers. It does not itself create new legal duties, though it may signal how the agency would enforce. A general statement of policy tells the public how the agency plans to exercise discretion in the future, without binding either the agency or the public.

Labels do not decide the question. Courts ask whether the document in substance creates new binding obligations, whether the agency treats it as binding when it acts, and whether it fills a gap in the statute by effectively amending a prior legislative rule. A policy statement that the agency applies as a rigid rule, never exercising discretion, may be a legislative rule in disguise, and so invalid if issued without notice and comment.

Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association (2015) held that an agency need not use notice and comment to issue a new interpretive rule that departs from an earlier interpretation. This rejected a D.C. Circuit doctrine, the Paralyzed Veterans rule, that had required notice and comment to change a definitive interpretation. The Court said the APA's text controls and courts may not add procedure. Note, however, that where a prior interpretation produced serious reliance interests, an agency changing course must still explain itself under the arbitrary and capricious standard.

The case also set up an argument about deference to interpretive rules and an agency's reading of its own regulations, which the Court later narrowed in Kisor v. Wilkie (2019), as the deference track explains.

Worked example: An agency issues a guidance letter telling regulated companies that a disclosure practice is unlawful and that it will bring enforcement actions against any firm that continues it. The agency has previously never taken that position and its field staff are told to bring cases without exception. A challenger would argue that the guidance imposes a new binding duty, so that it is a legislative rule that should have gone through notice and comment, and that labelling it guidance does not control. If a court agrees, the guidance is set aside as procedurally invalid.

lessons.title: Formal and Hybrid Rulemaking
body: Formal rulemaking is a trial-like version of rulemaking. Section 553(c) says that when rules are required by statute to be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing, the agency must follow sections 556 and 557 instead of the lighter notice-and-comment procedure. Those sections provide for an impartial presiding officer, oral evidence, cross-examination, a decision based exclusively on the record, and findings and conclusions on all material issues.

The trigger is the statute, not the agency's preference. Formal rulemaking applies only when Congress uses language about a hearing on the record. In United States v. Allegheny-Ludlum Steel Corp. (1972) and United States v. Florida East Coast Railway Co. (1973) the Supreme Court read a statute authorizing the Interstate Commerce Commission to set rates after hearing as not requiring on-the-record procedure. The Court held that the words after hearing, standing alone, did not trigger sections 556 and 557, and that Congress must use something closer to the statutory phrase on the record. Because of these decisions, formal rulemaking is rare. It is used in a small number of programs, such as certain Food and Drug Administration food standards.

The reason for its rarity is the time and expense. Cross-examination and a closed evidentiary record make rulemaking slow, and the famous example is a proceeding over the content of peanut butter that took years. Agencies and Congress therefore prefer informal rulemaking. Some statutes require hybrid rulemaking, an intermediate form that adds a few procedures, such as a public hearing or opportunity for rebuttal, to the notice-and-comment framework. Vermont Yankee prevents courts from adding such steps on their own, so hybrid procedures must come from a statute.

The rule against ex parte contacts is a good example of how process differs. In adjudication and formal rulemaking, section 557(d) bars communications between interested persons outside the agency and agency decision-makers about the merits, outside the record. In informal rulemaking there is no general statutory ban, though courts have sometimes required that critical information on which the agency relied be disclosed so commenters can respond, and the record should show it. The rule against prejudgment also differs: in rulemaking an official may have policy views but must not have an unalterably closed mind.

Agencies have an additional option under the Negotiated Rulemaking Act of 1990. The agency can convene a committee of representatives of affected interests to negotiate a consensus text, which the agency then proposes as a rule through ordinary notice and comment. Negotiated rulemaking does not displace section 553.

Worked example: A statute says the agency shall set standards for a food product after a hearing on the record. Under the Florida East Coast line of cases the court asks if the statute's wording meets the on-the-record standard. If it does, the agency must hold a trial-type hearing with cross-examination and decide on the record. If the statute says only after hearing, a court is likely to conclude that notice and comment suffices.

lessons.title: Formal Adjudication, ALJs and Due Process
body: Adjudication is the agency process for deciding a particular case, such as whether a company violated a statute or whether a person qualifies for benefits. The APA's formal adjudication rules apply to adjudications required by statute to be determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing (section 554). If that trigger is met, the hearing follows sections 556 and 557: notice of the issues, an impartial presiding officer, the right to present evidence and cross-examine, a decision based on the record, and a separation of functions within the agency.

Presiding officers are usually administrative law judges (ALJs). The APA protects them with removal only for good cause established by the Merit Systems Protection Board, and bars them from consulting parties on the facts without notice. Section 554(d) separates adjudicators from investigators and prosecutors within a case, but the agency head, who oversees both, is not subject to the separation. Withrow v. Larkin (1975) held that the combination of investigative and adjudicative functions in one agency does not by itself violate due process, because adjudicators are presumed honest and impartial.

Most agency adjudications are informal, meaning no statute requires a trial-type hearing. They may still be subject to the Constitution. The Due Process Clause protects life, liberty and property, and the first question is whether a protected interest exists. Board of Regents v. Roth (1972) held that property interests come from independent sources such as statutes or contracts, and that a person must have a legitimate claim of entitlement, not just a unilateral expectation. Goldberg v. Kelly (1970) held that welfare recipients with a statutory entitlement were entitled to an evidentiary hearing before benefits were terminated.

Mathews v. Eldridge (1976) supplies the test for what process is due. The court balances three factors: the private interest affected, the risk of erroneous deprivation under current procedures and the value of added safeguards, and the government's interest including the burden of added procedures. Applying it to a disability benefits termination, the Court held a pre-termination evidentiary hearing was not required, because the decision turned largely on medical records and a post-termination hearing was available. The test is flexible: more is due when the interest is weighty and the process is likely to catch errors.

Remember also the relevance of evidence rules. Formal adjudication permits hearsay, since the Federal Rules of Evidence do not apply. Richardson v. Perales (1971) held that written medical reports can be substantial evidence even if the doctors do not testify. Decisions must be supported by substantial evidence on the whole record.

Constitutional limits on agency adjudication have grown. In SEC v. Jarkesy (2024) the Court held that the Seventh Amendment requires a jury trial when the SEC seeks civil penalties for securities fraud, because the claim resembles a common-law action and the public rights exception did not apply. The decision has led to challenges to other agency penalty proceedings, and the boundaries of the public rights exception remain contested.

Worked example: A state agency tenured to a licensed physician proposes to revoke the license without a hearing. The license is a property interest created by state law. Applying Mathews, the private interest is high, the risk of error from decision without hearing is real, and the burden of a hearing is modest, so due process requires notice and an opportunity to be heard, at least before final revocation.

lessons.title: Choosing Between Rulemaking and Adjudication
body: The line between rulemaking and adjudication matters constitutionally, not just statutorily. Londoner v. Denver (1908) held that when a city assessed a tax on specific landowners based on facts peculiar to each, due process required notice and a hearing. Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board of Equalization (1915) held that no hearing was required when a board raised the valuation of all taxable property in Denver by the same percentage. The Court's reasoning is that where a rule applies to a large general group, individual hearings are impracticable and the affected people have their remedy in the political process. The usual framing: individualized, fact-specific decisions need process, and general policy choices do not.

Agencies often have a choice between making policy by rule and announcing it in an adjudication. The Chenery cases address that choice. In SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery I, 1943) the Court held that a reviewing court may uphold agency action only on the grounds the agency itself invoked. If the agency's stated reason is wrong, the court may not sustain the decision on a different rationale the court thinks was available. The agency may reconsider and reach the same result on proper grounds. This record-based rule remains central to judicial review and underlies why agencies must explain themselves in full.

In Chenery II (1947), after the SEC redid its order on a different ground, the Court held that an agency has discretion to choose between rulemaking and case-by-case adjudication in announcing new principles. The choice is the agency's, and is reviewed only for abuse of discretion. Adjudication has advantages when the agency cannot foresee all problems in advance, but a new rule announced in adjudication may unfairly surprise parties who relied on prior law.

Retroactivity is the limit. The APA's definition of a rule includes the phrase future effect, and Bowen v. Georgetown University Hospital (1988) held that agencies may not issue retroactive rules unless Congress has expressly given them that power. Adjudications, by contrast, are customarily applied retroactively to the parties, since a decision resolves a past dispute. Courts balance the harm to reliance against the statutory interest in applying the new standard, and they are especially concerned when penalties are imposed for conduct that was lawful under earlier agency precedent. Related due process doctrine limits fines for conduct the agency never gave fair notice was prohibited.

Another issue is whether agency adjudication creates precedent. Agencies are expected to follow their own precedents or explain why they depart. A change in position is permitted but the agency must acknowledge the change and give a reasoned explanation, a point developed in the review standards lesson.

Worked example: An agency has never required hospitals to report a type of incident. In an enforcement case against one hospital, it announces that the statute has always required reporting and imposes a large penalty. The agency may announce new principles in adjudication under Chenery II, but the hospital will argue lack of fair notice and unfair retroactivity, and a court may bar the penalty while still allowing the rule to apply going forward.

lessons.title: Reviewability, Final Agency Action and Preclusion
body: Judicial review of agency action is usually brought under the APA, sections 701 to 706. Section 702 gives a right of review to a person suffering legal wrong because of agency action, or adversely affected or aggrieved by it within the meaning of a relevant statute, and waives sovereign immunity in suits seeking non-monetary relief. The APA is not itself a grant of subject matter jurisdiction (Califano v. Sanders, 1977), so a plaintiff usually relies on federal question jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. 1331 or a special review statute that sends the case straight to a court of appeals.

Section 704 limits APA review to final agency action for which there is no other adequate remedy in court. Bennett v. Spear (1997) states a two-part test for finality. The action must mark the consummation of the agency's decision-making process, so it is not tentative or interlocutory, and it must be one by which rights or obligations have been determined or from which legal consequences will flow. A preliminary staff report fails the first part. A compliance order carrying penalties for noncompliance passes. Courts also take a pragmatic approach, as in the cases that treat agency orders with serious practical consequences as final.

Section 701(a) removes two classes of action from review: those where a statute precludes review, and those where action is committed to agency discretion by law. Preclusion can be express or implied from the statute's structure, but courts apply a strong presumption favoring review, drawn from Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner (1967), and require clear and convincing evidence of legislative intent to bar it.

Committed to agency discretion is a narrow exception. In Citizens to Preserve Overton Park, Inc. v. Volpe (1971), the Court said it applies only in rare circumstances where the statute is drawn so that a court would have no meaningful standard against which to judge the agency's exercise of discretion. In Heckler v. Chaney (1985), the Court held that an agency's decision not to take an enforcement action is presumptively unreviewable, because it involves a balance of factors, such as resources and priorities, that agencies are better placed to weigh. The presumption can be rebutted where the statute provides guidelines for enforcement or where the agency has adopted a general policy that amounts to abdication of its statutory duties.

Contrast refusals to enforce with rulemaking or licensing decisions, which are generally reviewable. A related distinction separates a refusal to act at all from a discrete, required act, which can be compelled. Section 706(1) lets a court compel agency action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed, but only where the agency failed to take a discrete action it is legally required to take (Norton v. Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, 2004).

Another important limit is the record rule. Review is on the administrative record that was before the agency when it decided, not on a new record developed in court (Camp v. Pitts, 1973). Courts may allow limited discovery only on a strong showing of bad faith or incompleteness of the record.

Worked example: A citizens group asks an agency to bring enforcement action against a company for violating an environmental statute. The agency declines without explanation. Under Heckler v. Chaney the refusal is presumptively unreviewable, so the group would need to show that the statute supplies enforcement guidelines, or that the agency announced a policy of non-enforcement that abdicated its statutory responsibilities. If the agency had instead denied a permit application, the denial would be a final, reviewable action.

lessons.title: Standards of Review: Arbitrary and Capricious, Substantial Evidence, De Novo
body: Section 706 tells a court what to do when it finds that agency action is unlawful. The standards differ by the kind of question and the type of proceeding.

Questions of law, such as what a statute means, are reviewed by the court without deference to the agency's view. Section 706 directs the court to decide all relevant questions of law, and in 2024 Loper Bright confirmed that this means independent judgment, as the next track explains. Section 706(2)(B) covers actions contrary to constitutional right, 706(2)(C) covers action in excess of statutory jurisdiction or authority, and 706(2)(D) covers action taken without observance of procedure required by law.

Findings of fact in formal proceedings, whether rulemaking or adjudication on the record, are reviewed under section 706(2)(E) for substantial evidence. Universal Camera Corp. v. NLRB (1951) explains that substantial evidence means such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion, and that the court must consider the whole record, including evidence that detracts from the agency's finding, not only the evidence that supports it. In practice the standard is deferential.

Most agency action falls under section 706(2)(A), which requires a court to hold unlawful and set aside agency action found to be arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law. Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm (1983) is the leading case. A court may not substitute its judgment for the agency's, but it will find a rule arbitrary and capricious if the agency relied on factors Congress did not intend it to consider, entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem, offered an explanation that runs counter to the evidence, or is so implausible that it could not be ascribed to a difference in view or the product of agency expertise. In State Farm the agency's rescission of an automatic restraint rule failed because the agency did not consider an alternative, an airbag-only requirement, that was within the ambit of the existing rule.

Reasoned decision-making demands more when an agency changes course. FCC v. Fox Television Stations (2009) held that the agency need not show that its new policy is better than the old, but it must display awareness that it is changing position and give good reasons, and it must take into account serious reliance interests that the old policy engendered. Department of Commerce v. New York (2019) refused to defer to the stated rationale for adding a citizenship question to the census, because the evidence showed the stated reason was contrived, which shows that the court will review whether an explanation is genuine. A pretext is not a reasoned basis.

Ohio v. EPA (2024) is a recent application. The Court stayed an EPA rule because the agency likely failed to respond adequately to comments arguing that the rule would not work if a part of it were removed. The case reinforces that agencies must respond to significant comments.

De novo review applies in only a few situations: when a statute provides for it, and in the rare case when agency fact-finding procedures are inadequate in an adjudication (Overton Park). Factual findings in informal rulemaking are reviewed under the arbitrary and capricious standard rather than the stricter substantial evidence standard, though the difference may be small in practice.

Remedy: section 706(2) says the court shall hold unlawful and set aside. Courts often vacate and remand, though they sometimes remand without vacatur when vacatur would be disruptive and the agency may cure the defect. Whether a court may vacate a rule universally rather than as applied to the plaintiffs is debated among Justices.

Worked example: A agency repeals a safety rule with a short explanation, ignoring comments showing the safety rule had prevented serious injuries and without noting its reversal of an earlier finding. Under State Farm and Fox the repeal is vulnerable as arbitrary and capricious, because it failed to consider an important aspect and did not explain the change in position.

lessons.title: Standing and the Zone of Interests
body: Article III limits federal courts to cases and controversies. Standing doctrine asks whether the plaintiff is the right person to bring the suit. Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992) states the three constitutional requirements. The plaintiff must have suffered an injury in fact, which is concrete and particularized and actual or imminent, not conjectural or hypothetical. There must be a causal connection between the injury and the conduct complained of, so the injury is fairly traceable to the defendant. And it must be likely, not merely speculative, that a favorable decision will redress the injury. The plaintiff bears the burden of showing each element at the stage of the case, so a complaint at the pleading stage needs plausible allegations while a summary judgment motion needs evidence.

Injury need not be economic. Aesthetic, environmental and recreational harm count, but a plaintiff must show personal use or enjoyment of the affected area. In Lujan, plaintiffs who said they hoped to someday visit places where endangered species were affected lacked an imminent injury, because they had no concrete plans. The Court also rejected a citizen suit theory based on a general interest in seeing the law enforced, since a generalized grievance shared by all citizens is not a particularized injury.

The Court has relaxed some elements for certain plaintiffs. Massachusetts v. EPA (2007) held that Massachusetts had standing to challenge the EPA's refusal to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles, and said that states are entitled to special solicitude in the standing analysis because of their sovereign interests. The application of that special solicitude has been narrowed in later cases.

Intangible harms are subject to limits. Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins (2016) and TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez (2021) hold that a bare statutory violation is not enough, and the plaintiff must show a concrete harm with a close relationship to a harm traditionally recognized as a basis for a lawsuit, such as reputational harm. In TransUnion, class members whose credit files were not disseminated lacked standing, while those whose false files were sent to third parties had it.

Recent decisions apply the doctrine against indirect plaintiffs. In FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024) doctors and medical groups challenging the FDA's loosening of rules on a drug lacked standing, because they did not prescribe or use it and their theory of injury depended on speculative downstream effects, and federal conscience protections already shield doctors from being required to perform or assist in abortions. United States v. Texas (2023) held that states lacked standing to challenge federal immigration enforcement priorities, because a plaintiff generally has no judicially cognizable interest in the prosecution of someone else.

Beyond Article III, the plaintiff must satisfy the zone of interests test, which is a requirement of the APA's cause of action. Association of Data Processing Service Organizations v. Camp (1970) asked whether the interest sought to be protected is arguably within the zone of interests protected by the statute, and Lexmark (2014) treats it as a question of whether the plaintiff falls within the class of plaintiffs whom Congress authorized to sue. The test is lenient under the APA, as Bennett v. Spear emphasized, and is denied only when the interests are so marginal or inconsistent with the statute's purposes that Congress could not have intended to permit the suit.

Organizations may sue on behalf of members if the members would have standing, the interests are germane to the organization's purpose, and neither the claim nor the relief requires individual members' participation (Hunt v. Washington State Apple Advertising Commission, 1977). Summers v. Earth Island Institute (2009) requires that the organization identify at least one specific member who is harmed.

Worked example: A grocery chain sues to challenge an agency approval of a competitor's product that it says is unsafe. The chain argues it will lose sales. Injury in fact is plausible, but traceability and redressability require facts showing that consumers would buy less from the chain because of the approval, and the zone of interests test asks whether the safety statute protects competitors, which is doubtful.

lessons.title: Ripeness, Exhaustion, Mootness and Timing
body: Timing doctrines decide when a court will hear a challenge. They sit alongside standing and finality and overlap with them.

Ripeness asks whether a dispute has matured enough for a court to decide it. Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner (1967) sets a two-part test: the fitness of the issues for judicial decision, and the hardship to the parties of withholding court consideration. In Abbott, drug manufacturers could challenge a labeling regulation before enforcement. The question was legal, the regulation was final, and waiting would force them to choose between costly compliance and risking penalties. By contrast, Ohio Forestry Association, Inc. v. Sierra Club (1998) held that a challenge to a forest management plan was not ripe, because the plan itself did not authorize any logging and further agency steps would come, at which point the group could bring a challenge. Purely legal questions that need no further factual development are ripest.

Exhaustion of administrative remedies requires a party to use the agency's own procedures before going to court. The aim is to let the agency correct itself, to develop a record, and to use expertise. Under the APA, Darby v. Cisneros (1993) held that a plaintiff need not exhaust optional appeals when the statute or rule does not require exhaustion and the agency action is already final and operative. Where a statute requires exhaustion, a court enforces it. Courts may excuse exhaustion where the agency lacks power to grant relief, where it would be futile, or where there is irreparable harm, though recent cases are strict about such exceptions. Axon Enterprise, Inc. v. FTC (2023) held that a party facing an agency enforcement proceeding may bring a structural constitutional challenge to the agency's existence in district court, rather than waiting for review in the court of appeals after the agency finishes, because the harm of being subjected to an unconstitutional proceeding cannot be undone later.

Primary jurisdiction is a related doctrine used when a court case raises an issue within the special competence of an agency. The court may stay its hand and refer the issue to the agency. Unlike exhaustion, it concerns a case already in court on a nonadministrative claim.

Mootness is standing over time, since the controversy must remain live. A case becomes moot when circumstances change so that the court can no longer grant relief. A defendant's voluntary cessation of the challenged conduct does not moot a case unless it is absolutely clear the conduct could not reasonably be expected to recur (Friends of the Earth, Inc. v. Laidlaw, 2000). Exceptions also exist for conduct capable of repetition yet evading review. These rules matter when an agency rescinds a challenged policy after being sued.

Limits on time to sue are set by statute. Many review statutes give a short period, such as 60 days. For APA claims with no specific review statute, the general six-year statute of limitations for civil actions against the United States, 28 U.S.C. 2401(a), applies. Corner Post, Inc. v. Board of Governors (2024) held that a claim under the APA accrues when the plaintiff is injured, not when the rule was issued, so a business created years after a rule took effect may still challenge it within six years of its injury. This opens old rules to challenge by newly formed plaintiffs.

Worked example: A company receives an agency's letter stating that its product will be treated as a banned substance, and warning of penalties. No enforcement has started. Under Abbott, the legal question of classification is fit for decision, and the company faces a dilemma of heavy compliance costs or risking penalties, so the challenge is likely ripe. If instead the agency had merely announced that it was studying the issue, a court would find the matter unripe.

lessons.title: From Skidmore to Chevron: The History of Deference
body: Statutes are often ambiguous, and agencies must read them to do their work. Who gets the last word on what an ambiguous statute means, the agency or the court? The answer has changed over time, and the history explains the present law.

Before 1984 the dominant approach was Skidmore deference, from Skidmore v. Swift & Co. (1944). A court gave an agency's interpretation weight in proportion to its power to persuade, looking at the thoroughness of the agency's consideration, the validity of its reasoning, its consistency with earlier and later pronouncements, and all the factors that give it power to persuade. It was respect, not a binding rule. The court decided the statute's meaning and treated the agency as a respected source.

Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc. (1984) changed this. The EPA had adopted a bubble concept for pollution sources under the Clean Air Act, and the Court upheld it. Justice Stevens set out a two-step test. At step one, the court asks whether Congress has directly spoken to the precise question at issue. If the intent of Congress is clear, that is the end of the matter. At step two, if the statute is silent or ambiguous on the specific issue, the question for the court is whether the agency's answer is based on a permissible construction of the statute. The theory was that ambiguity amounts to an implicit delegation to the agency to fill the gap, and that agencies have expertise and political accountability that courts lack.

Chevron was soon limited in several ways. United States v. Mead Corp. (2001) held that Chevron applies when Congress has delegated authority to the agency to make rules carrying the force of law, and the agency's interpretation was promulgated in the exercise of that authority, as in notice-and-comment rulemaking or formal adjudication. Informal documents such as a tariff classification letter were left to Skidmore weight. This threshold question was called step zero. Christensen v. Harris County (2000) had similarly denied Chevron to opinion letters.

National Cable & Telecommunications Association v. Brand X Internet Services (2005) held that an agency's reasonable interpretation under Chevron could override a prior judicial interpretation of the same statute, unless the court's earlier decision held that the statute unambiguously required its reading. This meant that agencies, not courts, controlled the meaning of ambiguous statutes over time.

The major questions strand emerged as an exception. In FDA v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. (2000) the Court declined to defer to the FDA's claim of authority to regulate tobacco, reasoning that Congress could not have meant to delegate a decision of such economic and political significance in so indirect a way, and that for extraordinary cases a court should hesitate before reading an ambiguous grant of authority to confer vast power. King v. Burwell (2015) applied the idea to refuse Chevron deference on a question of deep economic and political significance in the Affordable Care Act, though the Court then decided the issue itself.

By the 2010s, several Justices questioned Chevron, with critics pointing to the APA's instruction that the reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law, and to separation of powers concerns. Justice Gorsuch, then a circuit judge, argued in a 2016 concurrence that Chevron let the executive branch absorb power that belongs to the courts. Courts also grew uneven in how they applied step one. In practice the Court itself rarely used the Chevron framework in its later years, deciding many statutory cases without citing it. The setting was ready for a direct challenge.

Worked example: An agency regulation, issued after notice and comment under a delegation of rulemaking power, defines a statutory term in a way that the text can plausibly bear. Before 2024, a court would proceed to Chevron step one, find ambiguity, and then ask only whether the reading was reasonable. If the agency had expressed the same view in an informal letter, Mead would route the case to Skidmore.

lessons.title: Loper Bright and the Law Today
body: In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024), decided together with Relentless, Inc. v. Department of Commerce, the Supreme Court overruled Chevron by a vote of six to two in Loper Bright, with Justice Jackson recused, and six to three in Relentless. The case involved fishing companies challenging a National Marine Fisheries Service rule that required them to pay for observers aboard their vessels. Chief Justice Roberts wrote for the majority.

The Court's reasoning rested on the APA. Section 706 says the reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law and interpret statutory provisions. The Court said this reflects the traditional judicial role: courts exercise independent judgment about what the law is, and the fact that a statute is ambiguous does not mean Congress delegated interpretive power to the agency. Ambiguity is a normal feature of statutes, and resolving it is a legal question for courts. The Court also said that Chevron's presumption of implicit delegation was a fiction, that agencies have no special competence at resolving statutory ambiguities, and that Chevron had proved unworkable.

What replaced it? A court must exercise independent judgment in deciding whether an agency has acted within its statutory authority, using the traditional tools of statutory construction. The Court said that courts may, as before Chevron, seek aid from the interpretations of those responsible for implementing particular statutes, and that Skidmore respect remains, especially for interpretations issued contemporaneously with the statute and consistently maintained over a long period, which may be especially useful where a statute's meaning rests on factual matters within the agency's expertise.

The decision does recognize a continuing form of delegation. When Congress expressly delegates discretionary authority, using terms like appropriate or reasonable, or authorizes the agency to define a term, the court's role is to determine the boundaries of the delegation and to ensure the agency has engaged in reasoned decision-making within it. So the answer to who decides is the court for the statute's best meaning, unless the statute itself gives the agency discretion, in which case the court polices the limits. The majority also held that prior cases decided under Chevron remain subject to statutory stare decisis, so the holdings of those cases are not overturned just because Chevron fell, and reliance on Chevron alone is not a special justification for reopening them.

The effects continue to unfold. Challengers have sought to reopen older rules, though the Corner Post decision on timing and the stare decisis point limit this. Lower courts have applied Loper Bright to strike down interpretations in a number of settings. In McLaughlin Chiropractic Associates v. McKesson Corp. (2025) the Court held that district courts in enforcement proceedings are not bound by the FCC's interpretation of the Telephone Consumer Protection Act under the Hobbs Act, and must independently interpret the statute, applying Loper Bright. Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County (2025) emphasized substantial deference to agencies on the factual and policy aspects of environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act, showing that deference to agency judgment remains where the question is one of fact or policy rather than meaning of the law. Learners should check recent decisions, since lower courts are still developing the line between law and discretion.

Worked example: A statute authorizes an agency to regulate any facility that emits a pollutant in a harmful amount, and the agency defines harmful amount to include any detectable quantity. Under Loper Bright, the court itself asks what the statute best means. If the statute assigns the agency discretion to determine what counts as harmful, the court asks if the definition lies within that boundary and whether the agency reasoned adequately. It does not defer simply because the term is ambiguous.

lessons.title: Agencies Reading Their Own Rules and the Major Questions Doctrine
body: A separate deference question arises when an agency interprets its own regulation rather than a statute. Bowles v. Seminole Rock & Sand Co. (1945) held that the agency's interpretation of its own regulation has controlling weight unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation. Auer v. Robbins (1997) reaffirmed this rule, and it became known as Auer or Seminole Rock deference. The rationale was that the agency that wrote the regulation is best placed to know what it meant.

Kisor v. Wilkie (2019) kept the doctrine but cut it back sharply. Justice Kagan's opinion said a court must first exhaust all the traditional tools of construction, and that deference is available only if the regulation is genuinely ambiguous. Even then the agency's reading must be reasonable, and the interpretation must also satisfy several further conditions: it must be the agency's authoritative or official position, not an ad hoc statement; it must implicate the agency's substantive expertise; and it must reflect fair and considered judgment, not a convenient litigating position or a surprising new reading that creates unfair surprise. Four Justices concurred only in the judgment, and Justice Gorsuch's opinion argued that Auer should be overruled in full. Loper Bright did not address Auer in terms, so as of this writing Kisor deference remains, and its fate is an open question that courts and commentators watch.

Another line of cases governs the scale of power an agency may claim. The major questions doctrine says that when an agency asserts power of vast economic and political significance, the court will not accept a vague or ancillary statutory grant and will require clear congressional authorization. Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA (2014) refused to read a statute to let the EPA require permits for millions of small sources, which would have given the agency vast authority to rewrite the law. West Virginia v. EPA (2022) used the phrase major questions doctrine and held that the Clean Air Act's generation shifting approach in the Clean Power Plan was not authorized, since the agency claimed an unheralded power in a long-extant statute. Biden v. Nebraska (2023) held that the HEROES Act did not authorize broad student loan cancellation by the Secretary of Education, since a waiver authority to modify provisions did not clearly authorize forgiving about 430 billion dollars in debt.

The doctrine's justification is that Congress is presumed to make decisions of great economic and political significance itself, and the stakes of a claimed power are reason to doubt that Congress delegated it quietly. Critics argue that it lacks a clear trigger, invites judicial policymaking and conflicts with textualism. Defenders see it as a clear statement rule grounded in the separation of powers. The Court has not defined precisely what makes a question major, referring to factors like the amount of money, the number of people and the novelty of the claimed power, and the agency's lack of expertise in the area.

How do these fit together after Loper Bright? Major questions is a tool of statutory interpretation that comes before any deference: if it applies, the agency needs clear authorization. Otherwise, the court reads the statute for its best meaning. Skidmore and Kisor operate in narrower areas.

Worked example: A decades-old statute allows an agency to take measures necessary to protect public health. The agency invokes it to impose a nationwide requirement on millions of businesses, with a very large economic cost, in an area it has never regulated. Under West Virginia and Nebraska, a court asks whether the claimed power is of vast significance, and if so whether Congress clearly authorized it. A general phrase like necessary measures likely will not suffice.

lessons.title: The Freedom of Information Act
body: The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), enacted in 1966 and codified at 5 U.S.C. section 552, gives any person a right of access to records of federal agencies, subject to nine exemptions. The Supreme Court has described its basic purpose as ensuring an informed citizenry and checking against corruption, and has said that its exemptions are to be read narrowly, with the burden on the agency to justify withholding.

FOIA applies to agencies in the executive branch, including independent regulatory agencies and the Executive Office of the President units that exercise substantial independent authority, but not to Congress, the federal courts, or the President's immediate personal staff and advisers. It does not apply to state or local governments, which have their own public records laws.

The statute has several parts. Agencies must publish certain materials in the Federal Register, such as rules and statements of organization. They must make available for public inspection final opinions in adjudications, policy statements and staff manuals that affect the public, and frequently requested records. And any person may make a request for records reasonably described, following agency procedures. The agency must determine within 20 working days whether to comply and notify the requester of its determination. Requesters may be charged fees that vary by category of requester, with reduced fees for news media and educational users, and fee waivers if disclosure is in the public interest. Requesters may appeal and then sue in district court, where review is de novo and the agency bears the burden of justifying withholding.

The nine exemptions are exclusive. Exemption 1 covers properly classified national security information. Exemption 2 covers internal personnel rules and practices. Exemption 3 covers matters made confidential by another statute that meets certain criteria. Exemption 4 covers trade secrets and commercial or financial information that is privileged or confidential. In Food Marketing Institute v. Argus Leader Media (2019), the Court held that commercial information is confidential at least where it is customarily kept private by its owner and provided to the government under an assurance of privacy, rejecting a requirement of competitive harm. Exemption 5 covers inter-agency or intra-agency memoranda that would be privileged in civil litigation, including the deliberative process privilege, the attorney-client privilege and attorney work product. NLRB v. Sears, Roebuck & Co. (1975) explains that the deliberative privilege protects predecisional, deliberative material, but not final opinions, which are the agency's working law. Exemption 6 protects personnel and medical files where disclosure would be a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy. Exemption 7 protects certain law enforcement records on specified grounds, such as interference with proceedings or disclosure of confidential sources. Exemption 8 covers records on regulation of financial institutions. Exemption 9 covers geological and geophysical information about wells.

The FOIA Improvement Act of 2016 added a foreseeable harm standard: an agency may withhold information only if it reasonably foresees that disclosure would harm an interest protected by an exemption, or if disclosure is prohibited by law. It also limited the deliberative process privilege to records created fewer than 25 years before the request. Agencies must also release any reasonably segregable portion of a record after deleting exempt material. Courts review withholdings using an index or affidavit, called a Vaughn index after Vaughn v. Rosen (1973), that justifies each withholding. An agency may refuse to confirm or deny that records exist, known as a Glomar response, where the existence itself would reveal protected information.

The Court in Department of Justice v. Reporters Committee (1989) held that a compiled criminal rap sheet about a private individual could be withheld under privacy exemptions, since FOIA's core purpose is to shed light on what the government is up to, not on private citizens.

Worked example: A reporter requests an agency's internal draft memo recommending a policy and the final policy memo adopting it. The draft is predecisional and deliberative and may fall within Exemption 5, subject to the foreseeable harm requirement. The final memo that states the policy the agency actually adopted is working law and must be released.

lessons.title: Sunshine, Advisory Committees and the Privacy Act
body: FOIA is one of several statutes that govern government transparency, and each addresses a different problem. Understanding the differences is a staple of the subject.

The Government in the Sunshine Act of 1976, codified at 5 U.S.C. section 552b, requires meetings of multimember agencies to be open to the public. It applies to agencies headed by a collegial body of two or more individuals, a majority of whom are appointed by the President with Senate confirmation. A meeting is a gathering of the members that conducts or disposes of agency business, and the Act requires advance public notice. Ten exemptions allow closing meetings for subjects like national security, personal privacy, trade secrets, and certain law enforcement and adjudicatory matters. The exemptions track FOIA's exemptions but not exactly. A single-head agency, such as a cabinet department, is not covered. Agencies may close meetings only after a recorded vote.

The Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA) of 1972 regulates committees created or used by the executive branch to obtain advice. It requires that these committees have a charter, give notice of meetings, open meetings in most cases, and keep minutes and make records available. The purpose is to prevent hidden influence by private interests over government decisions and to keep the number of committees in check. A group is covered if it is established or utilized by an agency and includes members from outside the government. Exemptions exist for committees composed wholly of full-time federal officers, and the Supreme Court has read the term utilized narrowly in Public Citizen v. Department of Justice (1989), to avoid applying FACA to every consultation.

The Privacy Act of 1974, codified at 5 U.S.C. section 552a, protects individuals in the other direction. It regulates how federal agencies collect, maintain, use and disclose records about individuals that are retrieved by name or identifier. It prohibits disclosure of such a record without the person's written consent, subject to a list of exceptions, one of which is disclosure required under FOIA. A person has the right to access and request amendment of their own records. Because the two statutes overlap, an agency considering a FOIA request for personal information must weigh the privacy exemptions of FOIA, namely Exemptions 6 and 7(C), and the Privacy Act's constraints. The Privacy Act does not override a FOIA obligation: if FOIA requires disclosure, the Privacy Act permits it.

The Federal Records Act, with the Presidential Records Act of 1978, governs the creation, retention and disposal of federal records. Presidential records are owned by the United States and become subject to FOIA five years after the President leaves office, subject to restrictions. These statutes matter because FOIA is useful only if records exist, and there is a separate law about keeping them.

How do these fit together? The APA requires rulemaking transparency by notice and comment. FOIA makes records available on request. The Sunshine Act opens meetings of collegial bodies. FACA opens advice groups. The Privacy Act protects individuals' data. Each has its own scope, exemptions, and enforcement, and a single scenario can raise all of them.

Worked example: A five-member commission meets to deliberate a pending enforcement matter in private, after a recorded vote and a notice that the meeting will be closed under the exemption for adjudicatory matters. A reporter objects. Under the Sunshine Act the commission may close the meeting if one of the exemptions applies and it follows the required voting and notice procedures. The reporter may still use FOIA later to request records of the meeting, subject to its own exemptions.

questions.prompt: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, what does it mean for an agency action to be ultra vires?
choices: The action exceeds the authority that Congress granted in the agency's enabling statute
The action was adopted without the notice-and-comment procedures that the APA requires for a legislative rule
The action was decided by a single official even though the agency's own internal rules assign such matters to a multimember board
The action was reviewed by the White House before it became final

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the best description of the APA's basic distinction between a rule and an order?
choices: A rule takes effect only after approval by a congressional committee, while an order takes effect on the agency's own authority alone
A rule is an agency statement with future effect, while an order is the final disposition of a matter other than rulemaking
A rule is issued only by independent agencies after a public hearing, while an order is issued only by executive departments in closed sessions
A rule binds the public, while an order binds only the agency's own employees and officers

questions.prompt: Under Franklin v. Massachusetts (1992), which statement about the President and the APA is correct?
choices: The President is an agency only when he acts through an executive order
The President is not an agency, but the APA requires him to consult the agencies he directs
The President is not an agency, so his own actions are not reviewable under the APA
The President is an agency, but his actions are exempt from the APA's notice requirements

questions.prompt: Congress creates a Bureau of Home Safety by statute and directs it to set safety standards for household appliances. The Bureau, citing a general interest in consumer welfare, issues a rule banning all sales of gas-fired water heaters, which the statute does not mention. A manufacturer sues. What is the strongest argument for the manufacturer?
choices: The Bureau is an independent agency, and independent agencies may never issue rules that directly burden private commercial parties without an act of Congress
The Bureau combined rulemaking and enforcement functions in one body, which the Constitution's separation of powers forbids in any single agency
The Bureau should have sought the approval of the President under the Appointments Clause before acting
The Bureau has only the powers conferred by its statute, and a general welfare purpose does not authorize a ban beyond the standards-setting authority granted

questions.prompt: The Department of the Treasury, headed by a Secretary the President may remove at will, and the Federal Trade Commission, led by commissioners with for-cause removal protection, both issue rules. Which statement is most accurate about their legal differences?
choices: The Treasury is an executive department under direct presidential control, while the FTC is an independent agency whose commissioners the President may now remove at will under Trump v. Slaughter (2026)
Treasury rules are subject to the APA and to presidential review, while FTC rules are wholly exempt from both because Congress created the FTC as an independent body outside the executive branch
The FTC must obtain OIRA clearance for every action it takes, while Treasury operates entirely free of White House review because it is an executive department
The Treasury holds inherent constitutional powers that the FTC lacks, because only executive departments may ever claim authority derived from Article II

questions.prompt: Which test did Chief Justice Taft state in J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States (1928) for evaluating delegations of legislative power?
choices: Congress may delegate only to a delegate who is a member of the executive branch and is confirmed by the Senate
Congress must specify every detail that the agency will later enforce
Congress may delegate only for a limited period, after which the delegation must be renewed by a new statute
Congress must lay down an intelligible principle to which the delegate is directed to conform

questions.prompt: In how many Supreme Court decisions has a federal statute been struck down on nondelegation grounds, and in what year?
choices: Six decisions, spread across the New Deal era and the wage-and-price-control cases of the 1970s
None, because the Court has only ever narrowed statutes by applying the constitutional avoidance canon
Two decisions, both in 1935, involving oil shipments and the National Industrial Recovery Act
One decision, in 1928, striking down the flexible tariff-setting statute that Taft's opinion had upheld

questions.prompt: What was the result in Gundy v. United States (2019)?
choices: The Court declined to decide the nondelegation question and dismissed the case as moot after the petitioner's sentence expired
A plurality upheld the delegation, with Justice Alito concurring in the judgment while signaling willingness to revisit the doctrine
The Court struck down the delegation by a unanimous vote as an unconstitutional transfer of legislative power to the Attorney General
A majority adopted a new and stricter test than the intelligible principle standard, requiring Congress to resolve all major policy questions itself

questions.prompt: Congress enacts a statute authorizing the Secretary of Health to issue regulations that are 'requisite to protect the public from imminent and serious health hazards,' and requires findings supported by evidence and a report to Congress. A trade group argues the statute is an unconstitutional delegation. Under the Court's current doctrine, how is the challenge most likely to come out?
choices: The challenge fails, because the statute states a policy goal and boundaries that satisfy the intelligible principle test
The challenge succeeds, because any statute that lets an agency set binding private obligations without specifying each regulated product violates Article I
The challenge succeeds unless the Secretary is confirmed by the Senate and also removable only for cause by the President
The challenge fails only if each of the Secretary's regulations is later approved by a joint resolution of Congress

questions.prompt: A statute lets a private trade association of coal producers fix minimum wages and maximum hours that bind competing producers, with no agency review. A competitor challenges it. Which argument is strongest?
choices: The statute violates the intelligible principle test only if the wage standard is expressed as a fixed number rather than a general policy
The statute is valid because private associations become agencies under the APA once Congress names them in the enabling statute
The statute is valid because Congress may delegate regulatory power to any entity, public or private, that has industry expertise
Private actors cannot be given regulatory power over competitors without governmental control, as Carter v. Carter Coal suggests

questions.prompt: Under the Appointments Clause, how are principal officers of the United States appointed?
choices: They are elected by the agencies they will lead
They are appointed by the courts of law and confirmed by the President
They are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate
They are chosen by the heads of departments and approved by Congress

questions.prompt: What did Lucia v. SEC (2018) hold about the SEC's administrative law judges?
choices: They are employees performing purely ministerial duties, so no constitutional appointment procedure applies to them at all
They are principal officers who must be nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate before hearing any case
They are officers, but the Appointments Clause was satisfied because the SEC's chief ALJ and staff had selected them through a merit process
They are officers of the United States, so appointment by agency staff rather than the Commission violated the Appointments Clause

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes Seila Law LLC v. CFPB (2020)?
choices: Congress may not insulate a single director who wields substantial executive power from at-will removal by the President
Congress may never give for-cause removal protection to any official who heads an agency, whether alone or as part of a board
Seila Law overruled Humphrey's Executor in full, so every independent agency with removal-protected leaders was held unconstitutional
The CFPB was struck down in its entirety, and all of its past actions were declared void as a result

questions.prompt: Congress creates a five-member Commission on Transport Standards, with members serving staggered terms and removable only for neglect of duty. The Commission may issue rules and bring civil enforcement actions in court. The President fires a member who is a political opponent without alleging neglect. The member sues for reinstatement. Which analysis best predicts the legal question the court must decide after Trump v. Slaughter (2026)?
choices: Whether the Commission qualifies as an agency at all, because the President may remove only the heads of bodies that are not agencies
